metadata.title: Chapter 14: Active/Passive Voice (कर्तरि आणि कर्मणि प्रयोग)
metadata.subject: Gujarati
learning_outcomes: Understand the fundamental difference between [DICT_GUJ_KARTERI|कर्तरि प्रयोग] (Active Voice) and [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|कर्मणि प्रयोग] (Passive Voice).
Identify the grammatical roles of the subject (कर्ता), object (कर्म), and verb (क्रियापद) in Gujarati sentences.
Transform sentences smoothly from Active to Passive voice and vice versa.
Comprehend the subtle nuances of voice usage in formal and literary Gujarati texts.

ai_context.learning_goal: To master the syntax and agreement rules governing voice in Gujarati, empowering students to write and speak with precision.
common_misconceptions: Students often confuse the subject and object markers (like 'એ' or 'થી') in Gujarati grammar.
Assuming verbs always agree with the grammatical subject regardless of the voice type.
Translating English passive voice rules directly into Gujarati without accounting for native post-positions.

blocks.title: The Mystery of the Broken Vase
blocks.body: Imagine walking into a pristine living room at Shine Academy. A priceless antique vase lies shattered on the Persian rug. The director rushes in and asks two people what happened. The first person says, 'આશિષે ફૂલદાની તોડી' (Ashish broke the vase). The second person says, 'આશિષથી ફૂલદાની તૂટી ગઈ' (The vase was broken by Ashish). Both sentences describe the exact same physical disaster, yet the spotlight shifted. In the first sentence, Ashish is the absolute star of the sentence. In the second sentence, the poor vase takes center stage while Ashish steps into the background shadows. Welcome to the fascinating world of [DICT_GUJ_KARTERI|कर्तरि प्रयोग] and [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|कर्मणि प्रयोग] in Gujarati grammar!

blocks.question: In the story, when the speaker says 'આશિષથી ફૂલદાની તૂટી ગઈ', who or what receives the primary grammatical focus?
blocks.explanation: In that sentence, the construction shifts attention to the object (the vase), making it a passive-like structure where the verb agrees with the object.

blocks.title: Concept 1: The Architecture of a Gujarati Sentence
blocks.body: Before we can manipulate voices, we must inspect the building blocks of a Gujarati sentence. Every complete sentence relies on three foundational pillars: the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYAPAD|कर्ता] (Subject/Doer), the [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|कर्म] (Object/Receiver of action), and the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYAPAD|क्रियापद] (Verb/Action). In Gujarati, the standard word order is Subject-Object-Verb (SOV), unlike English which typically follows SVO. For instance, in 'વિદ્યાર્થી પુસ્તક વાંચે છે' (The student reads a book), 'વિદ્યાર્થી' is the subject, 'પુસ્તક' is the object, and 'વાંચે છે' is the verb. The magic of voice lies in deciding *which* of these elements controls the gender, number, and person of the verb.

blocks.front: What is the standard word order in Gujarati sentences?

blocks.title: Concept 2: Unpacking [DICT_GUJ_KARTERI|कर्तरि प्रयोग] (Active Voice)
blocks.body: The [DICT_GUJ_KARTERI|कर्तरि प्रयोग] is the most natural and frequently used voice in everyday Gujarati conversation. In this structure, the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYAPAD|कर्ता] (subject) is in the nominative case (or takes standard markers depending on transitive/intransitive past tenses), and crucially, the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYAPAD|क्रियापद] (verb) directly agrees with the subject in gender (लिंग), number (वचन), and person (पुरुष). Let us examine an example: 'છોકરો કેરી ખાય છે' (The boy eats a mango). Here, 'છोકરો' is masculine singular, and the verb 'ખાય છે' matches it. If we change the subject to feminine plural—'છોકરીઓ કેરી ખાય છે'—the verb remains plural. Active voice emphasizes the agent performing the action.

blocks.title: Spotting the Agent
blocks.body: When analyzing active voice in past tense transitive verbs in Gujarati, watch out for the 'એ' (e) suffix attached to the subject (e.g., 'રામે રાवण मार्यो'). Even with this marker, if the verb aligns with the subject, it remains under active governance!

blocks.question: In the sentence 'માતા રસોઈ બનાવે છે' (Mother cooks food), which word does the verb 'બનાવે છે' agree with?
options: It does not agree with any word
blocks.explanation: In Active Voice (कर्तरि प्रयोग), the verb always agrees with the subject (कर्ता), which is 'માતા'.

blocks.title: Concept 3: Transitioning to [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|कर्मणि प्रयोग] (Passive Voice)
blocks.body: When the spotlight shifts from the doer to the receiver of the action, we enter the realm of [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|कर्मणि प्रयोग]. In this structure, three major transformations occur: 1. The subject takes an instrumental post-position like 'થી' (by) or 'દ્વારા' (through). 2. The [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|कर्म] (object) becomes prominent and loses any accusative case markers if applicable. 3. Most importantly, the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYAPAD|क्रियापद] (verb) ceases to agree with the subject and instead **agrees entirely with the object** in gender and number! For example, Active: 'રામે પુસ્તક વાંચ્યું' -> Passive: 'રામથી પુસ્તક વંચાયું'. Notice how 'વંચાયું' matches the neuter singular noun 'પુસ્તક'.

blocks.front: In Karmaani Prayog (Passive Voice), what does the verb agree with?

blocks.question: Transform the active sentence 'ચોર પકડાયો' or 'પોલીસે ચોર પકડ્યો' into passive structure. Which option is correct?
blocks.explanation: In the passive form, the subject takes 'થી' (પોલીસથી) and the verb agrees with the object 'ચોર' yielding 'પકડાયો'.

blocks.title: Concept 4: Exploring [DICT_GUJ_BHAVE|ભાવે प्रयोग] (Impersonal Passive Voice)
blocks.body: Sometimes, a sentence has an intransitive verb—meaning there is **no object** ([DICT_GUJ_KARMA|कर्म]) present at all! How do we handle voice when there is no object to shift the spotlight to? Gujarati grammar introduces a unique masterpiece called [DICT_GUJ_BHAVE|ભાવે प्रयोग] (Impersonal Construction). In Bhave prayog, the subject takes the instrumental marker ('થી'), and the verb is converted into a neuter singular form, regardless of the gender or number of the subject. For instance, Active: 'બાળક રડે છે' (The child cries) -> Bhave: 'બાળકથી રડાય છે' (It is cried by the child / Crying is done by the child). The focus shifts entirely to the state or feeling ([DICT_GUJ_BHAVE|ભાવ]) of the action.

blocks.title: The Golden Rule of Bhave Prayog
blocks.body: Remember: Bhave Prayog ONLY happens with intransitive verbs (અકર્મક ક્રિયાપદો) where no object exists. The verb defaults to third-person neuter singular (-ચું/-એ છે / -ાય છે).

blocks.question: Why is 'બાળકથી હસાય છે' classified as Bhave Prayog rather than Karmani Prayog?
options: Because there is no object in the sentence.
Because the subject is a child.
Because the verb is in the future tense.
blocks.explanation: Bhave prayog occurs precisely when the verb is intransitive (has no object), forcing the verb into a neutral impersonal state.

blocks.title: Comparative Analysis: The Three Pillars
blocks.body: Let us summarize our journey so far by comparing the three grand structures side-by-side using the root verb 'כתબ' / writing or 'કર' / doing. 1. **[DICT_GUJ_KARTERI|कर्तरि प्रयोग]**: Verb agrees with the Subject (कर्ता). Example: 'તેણે પત્ર લખ્યો' (He wrote a letter). 2. **[DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|कर्मणि प्रयोग]**: Verb agrees with the Object (कर्म). Example: 'તેનાથી પત્ર લખાયો' (The letter was written by him). 3. **[DICT_GUJ_BHAVE|ભાવે प्रयोग]**: Verb is impersonal (neuter singular), no object exists. Example: 'તેનાથી હસાણું' / 'તેનાથી બોલાયું'. Mastering this triumvirate unlocks complete command over Gujarati literary elegance.

blocks.front: Which prayog has NO object and uses a neuter singular verb?

blocks.title: Nuances in Literary Gujarati and Modern Usage
blocks.body: In contemporary Gujarati, speakers often lean heavily toward [DICT_GUJ_KARTERI|कर्तरि प्रयोग] for directness and simplicity. However, classical literature, legal documents, and formal reports frequently employ [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|कर्मणि प्रयोग] to maintain objectivity. For instance, instead of saying 'સમિતિએ નિર્ણય લીધો' (The committee took a decision - active), a formal report might state 'સમિતિ દ્વારા નિર્ણય લેવાયો' (A decision was taken by the committee - passive), emphasizing the action or the decision itself rather than pinning sole agency on the committee members. Recognizing these stylistic choices is a mark of advanced language proficiency.

blocks.question: In formal or official Gujarati writing, why might an author choose Karmani Prayog over Karteri Prayog?
options: To make sentences longer and more confusing.
To maintain objectivity and focus on the action/result rather than the doer.
Because active voice is grammatically illegal in official texts.
blocks.explanation: Passive voice shifts emphasis away from personal agency, creating a neutral, objective, and formal tone ideal for reports and literature.

blocks.title: Step-by-Step Transformation Formula
blocks.body: Transforming sentences in Gujarati is like following a chemical recipe. To convert an Active sentence to Passive: Step 1: Identify the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYAPAD|कर्ता] (subject). Append the post-position 'થી' or 'દ્વારા' to it. Step 2: Identify the [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|कर्म] (object). Ensure it stands clear without accusative clutter. Step 3: Modify the [DICT_GUJ_KRIYAPAD|क्रियापद] root by adding passive infixes (like 'આય' or 'વા') and ensure the ending matches the gender and number of the object. Practice this recipe across 20 verbs, and your brain will perform these conversions instinctively!

blocks.front: What post-position is typically added to the subject when converting Active to Passive in Gujarati?

blocks.question: Apply the formula: Convert 'ગાયે ઘાસ ખાધું' (The cow ate grass - active) into passive voice.
blocks.explanation: Subject 'ગાય' becomes 'ગાયથી', object 'ઘાસ' stays, and verb 'ખાધું' transforms to passive agreement 'ખવાયું' matching neuter singular 'ઘાસ'.

blocks.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
blocks.body: Even advanced learners stumble upon tricky edge cases. Pitfall 1: Confusing transitive and intransitive verbs. If you try to create a Karmani prayog with an intransitive verb like 'દોડવું' (to run), the sentence breaks grammatically because there is no object. You must use Bhave prayog ('દોડાયું') instead! Pitfall 2: Forgetting gender agreement. In Gujarati, inanimate objects also possess gender (masculine, feminine, neuter). Always verify the gender of the [DICT_GUJ_KARMA|कर्म] before finalizing your passive verb ending.

blocks.title: The Gender Detective Challenge
blocks.body: Before writing a passive sentence, point to the object and ask: 'આ નર છે, નારી છે કે નપુંસક લિંગ છે?' (Is it masculine, feminine, or neuter?). That single question prevents 90% of grammatical errors!

blocks.question: What happens if you attempt to use Karmani Prayog with an intransitive verb (અકર્મક ક્રિયાપદ)?
options: The sentence is ungrammatical because there is no object for the verb to agree with.
The verb automatically changes to future tense.
blocks.explanation: Karmani prayog requires an object. Without an object, you must use Bhave prayog.

blocks.title: Summary of Shine Academy's Mastery Blueprint
blocks.body: We have traveled from the shattered vase hook to the intricate mechanics of [DICT_GUJ_KARTERI|कर्तरि प्रयोग], [DICT_GUJ_KARMANI|कर्मणि प्रयोग], and [DICT_GUJ_BHAVE|ભાવે प्रयोग]. Remember that grammar is not a set of arbitrary prison bars; rather, it is the architectural blueprint of human thought. By mastering voice, you control where the listener's eyes gaze—whether upon the zealous doer, the affected object, or the pure emotion of the action. Continue practicing with diverse vocabulary to achieve true linguistic fluency.
